Garnishee Orders

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A victory for the poor

Summary:
Apartheid was dismantled in the early 90’s but it was replaced by another form

of apartheid – the utter widespread exploitation of the poor through illegal debt

recovery mechanisms. The chief culprit being the garnishee order. Despite major

funded investigations by universities, work by the SA law reform society,

widespread press, the government has done nothing to alleviate the suffering of

the poor as they were exploited by banks, attorneys, furniture stores and debt

collectors.

Lets not fool ourselves that this is an phenomena that only affects one segment of

the population (i.e. the poor) and not the normal Carte Blanche viewer. Industry

bosses who are compelled by law to make these garnishee deductions watch in

horror as their employees take home pay is virtually nill. Thousands of South

African’s have to deduct from their domestic workers salaries. Productivity has

to decrease because those exploited by illegal garnishee orders suffer. Strikes

and demands for extra wages can also be tracked back to take home pay of

employees.

Lets not forget that the garnishee order is a very good system if 1) there has not

been reckless lending and 2) if its done legally.

Now the landscape is going to change and not through the government who sat

on the sideline, aware of the situation but has done squiddly nothing.

We tell the remarkable story of how this ended up in a marathon high court

hearing. We hear first hand the breathless ways poor people were exploited and

we hear the judges wrath as he listened to tales and tales of exploitation. The

major hitters in this case were a dream team who all gave their services on spec

– a top advocate, Webber Wentzel, Wendy Appelbaum and Clarke Gardener.



Further information:
We have courtroom visuals which will help unpack the case but most

importantly we need to ask the NPA straight away what it is going to do to put

into action what the judge has ruled. It is estimated that at least 40% of

garnishee orders have been instituted in the wrong magisterial district which is

against the law now. The judge has said that now there has to be judicial

oversight to investigate whether the original loan was not recklessly lent and

whether the debtor can actually pay a garnishee order. Considering that each

month 40 000 garnishee orders are instituted, how is this possible?

We also hear how overseas countries conduct their business regarding garnishee

orders.

Keeping a pulse on the nation – we can be defined by the overall personal debt

this country suffers from. We now know that much of the debt that the poor

people carry is as a result of reckless lending and illegal debt recovery. It is a

vicious cycle. We think in the interests of a fair South Africa, we need to tell this

story and we can also brag about how Carte Blanche has kept a finger on this

pulse for it was our story 10 years ago that put a stop to an illegal 25% extra paid

to debt recovery attorneys by creditors who, instead of taking that loss, put it

back on their debtors debt and with recurring interest they became forever

caught in in a debt cycle they could never escape from.

Press Release:


Court Slams Credit Providers - Garnishee Orders
It’s been called a victory for the poor. In 2012 business woman Wendy Appelbaum discovered that garnishee orders had been obtained against some of the workers on her wine farm. She decided to fight for their rights. Three years later the Western Cape High Court has ruled in their favour, sending shock waves through the credit industry. Carte Blanche investigates a landmark ruling against predatory credit providers.


Script:



10 am, 8th of July, media legal teams and commentators assemble in court 9 of the Cape Town High court. Also present are legal aid clinic representatives and several of their clients – all awaiting a ruling that could turn the credit and debt recovery industries on its head. Under scrutiny, decades of financial exploitation of the poor, which finally galvanized civil society to take action.

LINK
Enter businesswoman and philanthropist Wendy Appelbaum who became enraged when she discovered that her farm workers had fallen victim to unscrupulous moneylenders and debt collectors

Wendy a well know figure who owns a wine estate in Stellenbosch and who sits on many boards around the country, found out that some of her farm workers had up to 80% of their salaries deducted from garnishee orders.

A garnishee order, also known as an emolument attachment order or EAO is a court order, which instructs an employer to deduct money from an employer’s salary to pay a debt. Wendy started investigating them.

Wendy: I got myself the national credit act and the magistrates court act, read them, put myself to sleep and woke up in the morning with an absolute growl in my belly that something had to be done about this.
John: Were you offended by it? Did you take it personally?
Wendy: I was outraged to be absolutely honest, at the unfairness of this practice.

She became further enraged when she read forensic reports into the extent of the abuse. Some estimates put the number of garnishee orders active in South Africa running to three million. One forensic study on a big company found that 30% of employees had them and some employees had up to 12 garnishee orders and took home negative zero pay packages.

John: who were the villains here? You say you were angry. Who were you angry with?
Wendy: There were two sets of villains. There were the moneylender and there were the debt collectors and often I think they work hand in hand and scratch each other’s backs but I think they equally evil.

Clarke Gardner heads up summit financial partners and his passion is taking on debt collectors in court who break the law.

John: To what extent has it been abused? How bad is the situation?
Clarke: The abuse is rife, John. If you gave me 10 garnishee orders as I have been saying since 2000, and put it in front of me, ill show you 9 that has broken the law.

Abuses include debt balances that skyrocket. He showed us one example of what happened to a R99 debt that escalated to R11764 following the legal costs linked to a garnishee order.

Clarke: And that’s the kind of abuse that does happen so it certainly is rife, the degree of abuse varies.

It was to Clarke's expertise, that Wendy turned.

Clarke: I got a phone call on the other side and in a deep, excited voice I heard this is Wendy and I want to talk to you about emolument attachment orders. She then entertained a colleague and myself, Barry, here at the farm and then I realized that this lady is for real. This lady is serious. There is huge passion behind it and she is going to make it happen.

An outraged Wendy knew that their was only one way to stop the abuses and that was to take on the Government, money lenders and collectors in the high court – something never been done before. But she needed numbers and there was no shortage of them at the nearby Stellenbosch University Legal Aid Clinic, which provides free legal services to poor people. One of their clients and who was to become an applicant in the court case was Angeline Arrison. She has four garnishee orders, three issued in one day, for loans she says she never applied for or received.

Angeline: For 25 years I have lived in his small house with my two children and my husband.

70% of Angeline’s gross income was attached by garnishee orders. She said that she felt pressurized to sign consent to judgment. Order.

Angeline: He came and said I must sign I because it is a court order from Kimberley.

Another applicant, Lucinda bailey went into debt after her husband passed away.

Lisinda: So I struggled alone with my kids. I have 2 kids and from that stage on, there was no food on my table, I couldn’t pay my children’s school fees.

She had four garnishee orders against her name. This was primarily a case of reckless lending. Her debt became over R8000 a month, which was more than her salary.

Wendy’s next task was to find an attorney who would represent the legal aid clinics and its clients. Webber Wentzel attorneys happily agreed to come on board on a pro bono basis, as did advocate Anton Katz.

Odette: It was obvious that this is a public interest case of magnificent proportions.

Odette and her team threw themselves into a years work, often working over weekends to prepare their case.

Odette: From the moment that we became aware of this case and we started the research, we saw the enormity of the problem. It was something that we just had to work on.

Wendy and her team wanted the legal aid clinics clients garnishee orders declared invalid as they were obtained in the wrong magisterial district, and no judicial oversight to had taken place on of every each garnishee order, which the debtors argued was necessary even though they had consented to the order. These safeguards would go a long way to curbing the abuses.

Wendy: The fact that this had to be brought by civil society in order to jerk the government to action, because I think there lack of care for the poor has been extraordinary.

LINK
The government, despite being aware of the extent of the garnishee order abuses and the untold suffering that it causes has done very little to intervene. But now its hand has been forced.

Various government departments were included as respondents because garnishee orders and reckless lending were their areas of responsibility. The main respondent was Flemix and Associates, a law firm, whose director, Miss Jordaan was in court, and a number of credit providers. Flemix is the debt-collecting attorney of the 13 credit providers who were also sued.

Flemix’s primary business is collecting outstanding debts via garnishee orders. They have 150 000 active cases with a book value of 1.5 billion rand. It might have been an awkward moment in court when on the first day, the director, Miss Jordaan, happened to sit next to Wendy Appelbaum.

The court sat for a grueling 9 days. The judge was told about forum shopping. Flemix would gain garnishee orders from garnishee orders friendly magistrate courts instead of in the jurisdictions of the debtors.

Clarke: What we believe happens is that the debt collector has relationship in that court or they have found a weakness in that court or perhaps a vulnerable clerk of that court who stamps these with far greater ease than in another.

It would be several weeks before Wendy and her team would hear judge’s ruling.

John: How were you feeling? Confident?
Wendy: I was feeling confident in fact I think I was the one who was most confident throughout other than I think that the judge clearly throughout the case absolutely horrified throughout the case about what he was hearing.

LINK
Central to this case is the concept of consent to judgment. Why would any debtor agree to installments that they simply could not afford or for the matter to be heard in a court that they have absolutely no access to.

And that is exactly what the judge said when he dismissed set aside the garnishee orders against the applicants as they were unlawful. He ruled that the legislation allowing garnishee orders to be obtained with the debtor's consent was unconstitutional because it didn't provide for judicial oversight.

Wendy and their team got what they wanted. The judge also ordered that a copy of the judgment be forwarded to the law society to investigate whether Flemix had breached its ethical duties in respect of forum shopping to secure garnishee orders.
Judge Desai called this practice “the most disturbing feature of this matter”, declaring that the law could not be interpreted to allow forum shopping.

For Lisinda and Angelina, a moment of joy. They will find some financial relief as their Flemix garnishee orders are squashed.

Lisinda: I did cry because I was so happy there is someone who is listening. Someone who did care for us.

News quickly spread on the streets.

Wendy: I think it is a victory for the poor and I think that was really what we were doing was trying to give access to the law for the poor.

In the meantime Flemix is appealing the judgment and point out that the court's orders are suspended until the case is heard by the Constitutional Court. They say Judge Desai was wrong in his interpretation of the law, and that "the practical effect of the judgment is regrettable because the costs of collection that consumers will have to pay will be greatly increased if the judgment is upheld".

Marius Jonker heads up ADRA, the association of debt recovery agents.

Marius: The Stellenbosch judgment only effects the EAO granted against the consumers before court. There have been media reports that all these orders are unlawful now. That is not the case.

That may be so but time will tell if debt collectors are going to tow the line following judge Desai’s groundbreaking judgment.

Odette: I'm a very positive person and I would hope so.
John: Is that likely?
Odette: Is it likely, I don’t know.
